So this is the thing I'm most proud of. In March 2020 everything closed, and the district basically said okay, everybody's on Canvas now, good luck. And most of us had used Canvas for like posting homework and that's it. Our science stuff was all hands-on labs, so it just did not translate.

So I started building units. At first it was just for my own kids. I'd take a unit, like forces and motion, and break it into these short modules: a phenomenon video at the start, a little check-in question, then a simulation or an at-home lab with stuff from the kitchen, then a discussion post, then a short quiz that gave feedback right away. I kept every module the same shape so the kids always knew where to click. That was honestly the biggest lesson, consistency. Twelve-year-olds at home on a Chromebook with their little brother on the couch do not need creativity in the navigation.

Then two other teachers, one from my school and one from another middle school, asked if they could copy my stuff, and then we just started building together. So it was three of us and I was the one setting the template and checking everything, deciding the structure. We worked from April through December 2020, a lot of nights. By the end we had 36 units, covering sixth, seventh and eighth grade science. Each unit had the modules, a teacher guide, a materials list for home labs, and the Spanish versions of the student pages for a lot of them, because we have a big Spanish-speaking population. I did accessibility too, captions on all the videos, alt text, checked contrast, reading level. I learned a lot of that the hard way, from a kid with a screen reader.

Okay so then the district noticed. The curriculum office picked it up and honestly it got adopted district-wide, like it became the science curriculum on Canvas for the whole district. Well, okay, to be exact about it, officially it was a pilot, it went to three middle schools for the 2021-22 school year, that's about 1,100 students and fourteen teachers using it. Other teachers outside the pilot asked for copies and I shared them, so it was kind of everywhere, but the official thing was the three-school pilot. They talked about rolling it out to everyone and then the budget got weird and it stayed a pilot. I still think about that.

The results. The curriculum office tracked it a little. Module completion in Canvas was about 87 percent across the pilot classes, which for middle school is really good. On the common end-of-unit test, the pilot classes averaged about 6 points higher than the year before, but honestly that's comparing to a covid year so I wouldn't put too much on it. Teachers liked it, the survey was mostly positive, the main complaint was the quizzes were too long, so I cut them down.

And then the PD part. Because of the units I started running workshops for teachers on blended learning and Canvas course design. Between 2021 and 2023 I ran nine workshops, some on district PD days, some after school, and I think about 120 teachers came total. Honestly I feel like I trained basically every science teacher in the district at some point, it felt like that. But it's about 120 people across the nine sessions, and not all science, some were math and English teachers who wanted the template. I made a little self-paced Canvas course for the workshop too so people could go back to it.

I also published a cleaned-up version of the template and some of the units on GitHub, a friend who's a developer helped me set it up, it's called open-msci-units. It has the course template as a Canvas export, the unit design template, the rubric bank. People in other states have downloaded it, I don't know how many, I get emails sometimes.

What I learned from this, and why it matters for what I want now: I really like the design part. Figuring out the sequence, writing the questions, testing it with real kids, seeing where they get lost, fixing it. That's instructional design, I just didn't know the name for it in 2020. I've since done some reading on backward design and ADDIE and all of that, and I'm like oh, I've been doing this.
